Thank you. We added PL Trees, LinXGBoost and LightGBM linear-tree comparisons. On sparse regime slopes, frozen configurations won against Lin in all five new data draws (RMSE 0.3142 vs 0.4084). On the additive sparse task at n=240,d=32, CGB achieved 0.5426 vs Lin's 1.3097 across five fresh draws. These establish selective benefits beyond constant leaves.

The missing standard-score/predictive-leaf combination is LeafOnly. In the fixed-backbone four-way ablation, regime-slope RMSE was 0.5380/0.5929/0.3224/0.3020 for Bias/LeafOnly/SplitOnly/Full. Full vs LeafOnly isolates the scoring increment with predictive leaves present; Full vs SplitOnly isolates the leaf-model increment with predictive scoring present. Other mechanisms retain negative results. New Full-selected LeafOnly checks are reported separately from this controlled ablation.

CPU remains unfavorable. Several evaluated linear-leaf implementations are unstable there, but this does not establish a shared cause or absolve our method. Leaf support, coefficients and extrapolation are candidate explanations, not proven causes. We will clarify the observed failure and avoid presenting off-path feature use as a validated suitability rule.
drafts.t7wg:
Thank you. The contribution is the combination of routing-independent predictive candidates, predictive-aware histogram scoring and constant-or-single-slope leaves within boosting. The fixed-backbone 2x2 ablation separates scoring from leaf prediction; gains depend on the mechanism. We will sharpen the distinction from prior linear-tree formulations.

Practical benefit is selective. On NOX (600 training rows; five training repeats sharing a chronological test set), CGB reduced RMSE by 6.23% vs native PL Trees. At a prespecified seed, three same-machine timing repeats gave 7.90x faster fitting and 20.53x faster prediction of 14,542 rows. LinXGBoost and LightGBM linear trees were more accurate, so this is a trade-off.

Equal 300/900s search caps gave about 3% lower RMSE than XGB on kin8nm, but not on energy/CPU; final-refit costs are recorded separately. We do not claim broad compute-matched superiority.

k=1 is both a low-capacity bias and a cost choice. Across 35 fixed-routing probes, larger leaves helped dense/protein cases but hurt sparse cases. This is not joint k>1 retraining. We have no validated real-data suitability rule; the practical recommendation is to check validation quality and cost against strong alternatives.

drafts.wWos:
Thank you. We added direct PL Trees, LinXGBoost and LightGBM linear-tree comparisons, with fitting and prediction reported separately. The evidence supports targeted use rather than a default replacement for conventional boosting.

On sparse regime slopes, frozen configurations gave mean RMSE 0.3142 vs Lin's 0.4084 on five fresh data draws, winning all five. The additive sparse task also improved over every tested comparator in five fresh draws. CGB was slower to fit than native PL/LGB linear on that task, while the large speed gap to the author Python Lin implementation includes implementation differences.

A real working point is NOX: with 600 training rows and five repeats on one chronological test set, CGB's mean RMSE was 6.23% lower than native PL's. At a prespecified seed, three same-machine repeats measured 7.90x faster fitting and 20.53x faster prediction of the full 14,542-row batch. Lin and LGB linear retained lower error.

The equal-search-budget study is complete: kin8nm improved by about 3% at 300/900s, whereas energy and CPU did not benefit. Final-refit costs and incomplete-candidate outcomes are retained. Candidate count increases overhead; we will separate search, final fitting and inference costs and keep the unfavorable general-tabular results.
drafts.VVba:
Thank you. Within a fixed routing region, the boosted classification margin can be F(x)=b+sum_j a_j*x_j. Its zero set may be oblique, so axis-aligned routing does not force a staircase ensemble boundary. This concerns expressiveness, not a guarantee that training recovers that boundary.

Each leaf chooses one candidate w*x_j; x_0=1 provides a constant option. A constant candidate does not give every slope leaf a free intercept. The restriction controls local capacity while boosting accumulates updates. An affine w*x+b also has a 2x2 closed-form fit; we will not claim that it inherently requires expensive generic optimization. Our fixed-routing affine probes show benefits on regional-intercept tasks and deterioration on some sparse tasks, so no-bias is a trade-off.

Predictive-feature selection occurs at each leaf, while candidate pools are sampled per tree. This is an implementation/design choice, not a claim of superiority over node-level sampling. Independent role draws may overlap; explicit sharing reuses a pool. We will clarify that distinction.

p denotes predictive-candidate fraction; we will reconcile the rho notation. SplitOnly uses predictive-aware scoring with constant terminal leaves; p=1 offers all predictive candidates for scoring, not multiple predictors per leaf. CatBoost's stronger general-tabular ranking remains reported.
